title: Animal Organ Systems & Immunity

competencies.text: Explain nervous + endocrine coordination for temperature regulation.
Explain how vaccines work via immune and lymphatic systems.
Describe how damaged parts affect organisms (torn ACL, asthma attack).

days.title: Keeping Body Temperature Stable
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will explain how the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate temperature regulation, explain how vaccines work through the immune and lymphatic systems, and describe how damaged parts affect the whole organism.

🌡️ Homeostasis at 37 °C

Enzymes work best near 37 °C, so the body keeps its temperature in a narrow range. The hypothalamus in the brain acts like a thermostat.

ConditionNervous system (fast)Endocrine system (slower, longer)
Too hotSweating; blood vessels in skin widen (vasodilation) to lose heatLess thyroid hormone → lower metabolism
Too coldShivering; skin vessels narrow (vasoconstriction) to keep heatMore thyroid hormone and adrenaline → more heat from metabolism

🔁 Negative Feedback

The response reverses the change: when you get too hot, sweating cools you; once temperature is normal, sweating slows. Nerves act in seconds through electrical signals; hormones act over minutes to hours through the blood. Together they give quick and lasting control.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: Which part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat?

choices.label: Hypothalamus
Cerebellum
Brain stem
Spinal cord nerves

scenario.explanation: The hypothalamus senses blood temperature and triggers nervous and hormonal responses.

scenario.text: Why does your skin look flushed after running under the sun?

choices.label: Skin blood vessels widen to release heat
Blood is producing much more oxygen
Sunlight colors the skin cells red
Muscles push the blood out through the skin

scenario.explanation: Vasodilation sends more warm blood near the skin surface so heat can escape.

scenario.text: How do the nervous and endocrine responses differ?

choices.label: Nerves act in seconds; hormones act longer
Hormones act in seconds; nerves act longer
Both act only while a person is asleep
Nerves use blood; hormones use electricity

scenario.explanation: Nerve signals are fast electrical impulses; hormones travel in the blood and have slower, longer-lasting effects.

days.title: Body Defenses and Vaccines
days.content:
🛡️ Three Lines of Defense

LineWhat it includes
1st — barriersSkin, mucus, cilia, tears, stomach acid
2nd — general responseInflammation, fever, white blood cells that engulf germs
3rd — specific immunityB cells make antibodies; T cells kill infected cells; memory cells remember the germ

🧫 The Lymphatic System

Lymph vessels collect fluid from tissues and return it to the blood. Lymph nodes filter this fluid and are where many white blood cells meet germs. Swollen nodes in the neck during a sore throat show the immune system at work.

💉 How Vaccines Work

  1. A vaccine contains a weakened or killed germ, or a harmless piece of it (an antigen).
  2. The immune system responds: B cells make antibodies and memory cells form.
  3. If the real germ enters later, memory cells recognize it and respond quickly and strongly, so the person does not get seriously ill.

When most people are vaccinated, germs cannot spread easily, which also protects babies and the sick — herd immunity.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.right: Brain region that controls body temperature
Skin blood vessels widen to lose heat
match.why: It happens when the body is too hot.

match.right: Skin blood vessels narrow to keep heat
match.why: It happens when the body is cold.

match.right: Skin, mucus, tears and stomach acid
Remember a germ for a faster future response
Filter lymph and house white blood cells
Many vaccinated people protect the unvaccinated

days.title: When a Part Is Damaged
days.content:
🦵 Torn ACL

The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) connects the thigh bone to the shin bone and keeps the knee stable. It often tears in basketball or volleyball when a player lands or pivots suddenly. Effects: pain, swelling, a knee that "gives way," and inability to play. Because movement drops, muscles weaken and the person may gain weight — one injured part affects the whole body. Treatment includes rest, physical therapy and sometimes surgery.

🌬️ Asthma Attack

In asthma, the bronchioles become inflamed, muscles around them tighten, and extra mucus forms. Airways narrow, causing wheezing and shortness of breath. Less oxygen reaches the blood, so the heart beats faster and the person feels weak or anxious. Triggers include smoke, dust, pollen and exercise. A reliever inhaler relaxes the airway muscles.

🔗 The System Lesson

Damaged partDirect effectWider effect
ACLUnstable kneeLess movement; muscle loss
Bronchioles (asthma)Narrow airwaysLow oxygen; heart strain
KidneysPoor blood filteringWastes and fluids build up

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Apply homeostasis, immunity and system thinking. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A child got the measles vaccine. Weeks later she is exposed to measles but does not get sick. Why?

choices.label: Memory cells quickly recognized and fought the virus
The vaccine killed every virus in the whole barangay
Measles viruses cannot infect children who eat well
The vaccine made her skin too thick for viruses

scenario.explanation: The vaccine trained her immune system. Memory cells responded fast enough to stop the infection.

scenario.text: A volleyball player tears her ACL. Besides knee pain, what wider effect is MOST likely after weeks of little movement?

choices.label: Leg muscles weaken from lack of use
Her lungs stop exchanging oxygen
Her knee grows a brand-new ligament
Her blood type changes from A to O

scenario.explanation: Reduced activity causes muscle loss — a damaged part affects other systems.

scenario.text: During PE, a student with asthma wheezes and struggles to breathe. What is happening inside?

choices.label: Bronchioles narrow, so less air reaches alveoli
Alveoli burst open and fill the lungs with water
The heart stops pumping blood to the lungs
The trachea grows larger to hold extra air

scenario.explanation: Inflammation, tight muscles and mucus narrow the bronchioles, reducing airflow and oxygen intake.

scenario.text: You step from an air-conditioned room into a hot street. Which response happens FIRST?

choices.label: Nerves trigger sweating and skin vessels widen
Thyroid hormone drops over the next few days
Your body grows extra sweat glands right away to cope
Your blood type changes to handle the heat

scenario.explanation: The nervous system responds within seconds; hormonal adjustments are slower.

scenario.text: A small cut on your finger turns red, warm and slightly swollen. What does this show?

choices.label: Inflammation — the second line of defense
The first line of defense working perfectly
An allergic reaction to air entering the cut
Memory cells from a recent vaccine working

scenario.explanation: More blood flow brings white blood cells to the site, causing redness, warmth and swelling.

days.title: Protecting the Whole System
days.content:
💉 Vaccines in the Philippines

The national immunization program gives free vaccines for diseases like measles, polio, tuberculosis (BCG), hepatitis B, diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis. Outbreaks of measles and polio return when vaccination rates drop — showing why herd immunity matters.

🏃 Supporting Homeostasis

  • Drink water during hot days — sweat removes water and salts.
  • Rest in shade if dizzy or overheated; heat stroke happens when cooling fails.
  • Warm-up and proper landing technique reduce ACL injuries.
  • Avoid asthma triggers such as cigarette smoke; keep a reliever inhaler nearby.

🧠 Thinking in Systems

The body is a set of linked systems. The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate; the immune and lymphatic systems defend; the muscular, skeletal, respiratory and circulatory systems keep us moving and supplied. When one part fails, the others are strained — so protecting each part protects the whole organism.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: What happens to blood vessels in the skin when you are cold?

choices.label: They narrow to keep heat inside
They widen to let more heat out
They burst to warm up the skin
They fill with sweat to trap heat

escape.explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, so less heat is lost.

choices.label: A weakened, killed or partial germ
A full dose of a strong live disease
Antibiotics that destroy all bacteria
Hormones that raise body temperature

escape.explanation: Vaccines use a harmless form or part of a germ so the immune system can learn to recognize it.

choices.label: B cells
Red blood cells
Platelets
Nerve cells

escape.explanation: B lymphocytes produce antibodies that tag specific germs for destruction.

escape.text: What is the role of lymph nodes?

choices.label: Filter lymph and help white cells meet germs
Pump blood around the whole body more quickly
Produce hormones that control body heat
Store air for breathing during exercise

escape.explanation: Lymph nodes filter fluid and are sites where immune cells detect and fight germs.

escape.text: A torn ACL directly affects which body part?

choices.label: Knee joint
Lungs
Elbow
Ankle bone

escape.explanation: The ACL is a ligament inside the knee that keeps it stable.

escape.text: Why does vaccinating most of a community protect babies who are too young for some vaccines?

choices.label: Germs cannot spread easily, so babies are less exposed
Babies absorb antibodies from their vaccinated neighbors
Vaccines given to adults travel through the air
Babies cannot catch any diseases until they walk

escape.explanation: Herd immunity: when most people are immune, the germ has few chances to spread, shielding those who are not immune.
